Strategic knowledge encoded for the `sts2-coach` Skill. Paraphrases publicly available content from **Baalorlord** ([Twitch](https://www.twitch.tv/baalorlord), [YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/@baalorlord)). Any misrepresentation is ours, not his — see ATTRIBUTION.md.

# General Strategy

## Four Pillars

Baalorlord's four fundamental pillars that every successful deck must address. A deck that is weak in any pillar will struggle. Evaluate your deck against these pillars after every card reward and shop visit.

### Damage Output

Your ability to deal damage to enemies. Split into two sub-categories: frontloaded damage and scaling damage. You need BOTH — frontloaded for hallway fights and early turns, scaling for long boss fights.

#### Frontload

Damage you can deal in the first 1-2 turns of combat without any setup. This is your bread and butter for hallway fights and the early turns of elite/boss fights.

**Importance:** Critical in Act 1 where you have no scaling yet. Hallway fights should ideally end in 2-3 turns. If fights drag on, you take unnecessary damage that limits your pathing options.

**Target:** Aim to deal 30-40+ damage in the first 2 turns by mid-Act 1. By Act 2, you want 50+ frontloaded damage available.

##### Examples

- Ironclad: Carnage, Pummel, Uppercut, Headbutt
- Silent: Backstab, Predator, Dash, Poisoned Stab
- Defect: Cold Snap, Ball Lightning, Doom and Gloom, Compile Driver
- Necrobinder: Osty attacks, Doom application cards
- Regent: Sovereign Blade (with Forge stacks), Star-powered attacks

**Common Mistake:** Ignoring frontload in favor of scaling. A deck full of scaling cards with no frontload will lose 30+ HP in hallway fights before the scaling comes online.

#### Scaling

Damage that grows over the course of a fight. Strength, Poison stacks, Focus + Orbs, Doom accumulation, Forge stacks — anything that makes each subsequent turn deal more damage than the last.

**Importance:** Essential for boss fights and tough elites that last 5+ turns. Without scaling, bosses become wars of attrition you will lose. The longer a fight goes, the more scaling matters.

**Target:** Have at least one reliable scaling source by the end of Act 1. By Act 2, you want 2+ scaling sources or one very strong one.

##### Examples

- Ironclad: Demon Form, Inflame, Spot Weakness, Limit Break
- Silent: Noxious Fumes, Catalyst, Envenom
- Defect: Defragment, Biased Cognition, Capacitor, Echo Form
- Necrobinder: Doom stacking, recurring Souls
- Regent: Star generation engines, Forge accumulation

**Common Mistake:** Over-investing in scaling without enough block or frontload. A Demon Form is worthless if you die on turn 2.

### Cycle Time

How quickly you see your important cards again. Cycle time is determined by deck size, draw, and card manipulation. A smaller, tighter deck with good draw sees its power cards every 2 turns instead of every 4.

**Ideal Deck Size:** 20-25 cards for most builds. Some exhaust-heavy builds can go larger (28-32) because they thin in combat. Some ultra-thin builds work at 15-18 but require specific synergies.

**Target Cycle:** See your full deck every ~2 turns. With a 20-card deck and 5-card hand, you see everything in 4 draws (2 turns). Add draw cards and it's even faster.

**Why It Matters:** If your deck has 35 cards and your win condition is 3 specific cards, you might not see them together for 5+ turns. That's 5 turns of taking damage without your engine running.

#### Tips

- Skip card rewards more often than you take them — every card you add increases cycle time
- Prioritize draw cards: they effectively reduce your deck size by letting you see more cards per turn
- Remove Strikes and Defends at every opportunity — they are the weakest cards in your deck
- Exhaust cards naturally thin your deck during combat, improving cycle time as the fight progresses
- Innate cards reduce effective cycle time by guaranteeing key cards in opening hand
- Retain cards improve consistency by letting you hold key cards across turns

#### Card Removal Priority

- Strikes first (they deal less damage than almost any common attack)
- Defends second (they block less than almost any common skill)
- Curses/Status immediately when possible
- Redundant copies of conditional cards

### Block Density

The percentage of your deck that can generate block. You need enough block cards to survive enemy attacks on most turns, but not so many that you can't kill enemies.

**Target Percentage:** 33

**Target Description:** Roughly 1 in 3 cards should generate block. In a 21-card deck, that's ~7 block cards. This ensures you draw at least 1-2 block cards per hand.

#### Tips

- Block cards that also do something else (Shrug It Off draws, Dash blocks AND attacks) are premium picks
- Don't neglect block in Act 1 — you need to survive elites and the Act 1 boss
- Strength/scaling builds still need block; you can't just race bosses
- Artifact and Intangible are the best 'block' in the game — they prevent damage entirely
- Calculate how much incoming damage you expect and whether your block density can handle it
- Dexterity increases the value of every block card — it's block scaling

#### Scaling Block

Block that grows over time, similar to damage scaling. Dexterity, Metallicize, After Image, Frost Orbs with Focus — these make your block better every turn.

##### Examples

- Ironclad: Barricade + Body Slam, Metallicize, Feel No Pain
- Silent: Footwork (Dexterity), After Image, Blur
- Defect: Frost Orbs + Focus, Glacier, Reinforced Body
- Necrobinder: Osty as meat shield, defensive Souls
- Regent: Star-powered block generation

### Upgrade Density

The percentage of your deck that is upgraded. Upgraded cards are significantly more efficient — they deal more damage, block more, cost less, or gain additional effects. Campfires are your primary upgrade source.

**Target Percentage:** 50

**Target Description:** Aim to have at least half your deck upgraded by Act 2. By Act 3, 60-75% upgraded is ideal. Upgrades are one of the most reliable ways to increase deck power.

#### Tips

- Upgrading is almost always better than resting at a campfire if you're above 50% HP
- Prioritize upgrading your most-played cards — cards you see every fight benefit most from upgrades
- Some upgrades are transformative: Bash+ applies 3 Vulnerable, Neutralize+ applies 2 Weak, etc.
- Calculate the total value of an upgrade over an entire run — an upgraded card played 50+ times adds up enormously
- Key upgrades that change card function (add draw, reduce cost, add effects) are highest priority
- Upgrades to 0-cost cards are often very efficient since you always play them

#### Upgrade Priority Framework

- 1. Cards that gain new effects when upgraded (cost reduction, added draw, new mechanics)
- 2. Cards you play every single turn (your most consistent damage/block sources)
- 3. Scaling cards (making your scaling faster or stronger compounds over a fight)
- 4. Cards that go from situational to always-good when upgraded
- 5. Cards with minor stat bumps (last priority — +3 damage is less impactful than a new effect)

## Card Evaluation

How to evaluate card rewards and decide what to take, skip, or remove.

### Jobs Framework

Baalorlord's 'Jobs' framework for card evaluation. Every card should fill a specific job your deck needs. Don't evaluate cards in a vacuum — evaluate them based on what your deck is currently missing.

#### Jobs

Deal immediate damage without setup

**Job:** Frontload Damage

**When Needed:** Always needed in Act 1. Check if your first 2 turns deal enough damage to kill small hallway enemies.


Grow damage output over a long fight

**Job:** Scaling Damage

**When Needed:** Needed before first elite, critical before first boss. If you have no scaling, prioritize this.


Prevent incoming damage

**Job:** Block Generation

**When Needed:** Always needed. If less than ~30% of your deck generates block, prioritize block cards.


See more cards per turn, improve consistency

**Job:** Card Draw

**When Needed:** Needed once deck size exceeds 20 cards. Critical if you have powerful cards you rarely see.


Handle multiple-enemy encounters efficiently

**Job:** AOE Damage

**When Needed:** Need at least 1 AOE source by mid-Act 1. Multiple enemy fights are common and dangerous.


Weak, Vulnerable, or other debuffs that reduce enemy effectiveness

**Job:** Enemy Debuffs

**When Needed:** Weak is always valuable (reduces damage by 25%). Vulnerable amplifies your damage by 50%.


Scry, retain, search, or otherwise control what you draw

**Job:** Deck Manipulation

**When Needed:** Becomes important in Act 2+ as fights become more complex and sequencing matters more.


#### Evaluation Process

- 1. Identify which jobs your deck currently needs most urgently
- 2. Evaluate each card reward by which job(s) it fills
- 3. Prefer cards that fill multiple jobs simultaneously (e.g., Shrug It Off blocks AND draws)
- 4. Skip the reward if no card fills a needed job — adding bloat is worse than skipping
- 5. Consider the next 3-5 fights: what do you need to survive RIGHT NOW?

### Two Cost Cards

Baalorlord emphasizes that new players chronically undervalue 2-cost cards. A 2-cost card that does 2 things is often more efficient than playing two 1-cost cards that each do one thing.

**Reasoning:** A 2-cost card takes 1 card slot in your hand and 1 draw to see. Two 1-cost cards take 2 slots and 2 draws. The 2-cost card is better for cycle time even if the raw numbers seem similar.

#### Examples

- Carnage (2 cost, 20 damage) vs two Strikes (2 cost total, 12 damage) — Carnage wins on damage AND cycle time
- Dash (2 cost, 10 damage + 10 block) replaces a Strike AND a Defend in one card slot
- Doom and Gloom (2 cost, 10 damage + channel Dark orb) provides damage AND orb value in one play

#### When To Avoid Two Cost

- When you have very limited energy (3 energy with no energy relics)
- When the 2-cost card's effect is too situational or conditional
- When you already have too many 2-cost cards and can't play your full hand

### Skipping Philosophy

One of Baalorlord's most important teachings: skipping card rewards is a powerful strategic tool. Most players take too many cards.

#### Key Principles

- Every card you add to your deck increases cycle time — make sure it's worth it
- A mediocre card is WORSE than no card because it dilutes your draws
- In Act 2 and Act 3, you should be skipping 40-60% of card rewards
- Ask yourself: 'Does this card make my deck better, or just bigger?'
- The best players skip aggressively and have tight, focused decks
- It's better to have a 20-card deck where every card is good than a 30-card deck with 10 filler cards

#### When To Take

- The card fills an urgent job your deck needs
- The card has exceptional synergy with your existing cards
- You're in Act 1 and need any reasonable damage or block
- The card is a rare/powerful card you'd build around

#### When To Skip

- No card fills an urgent need
- The cards are marginal upgrades over what you already have
- Your deck is already 25+ cards and you don't have exhaust mechanics
- Taking the card would reduce your consistency more than it adds power

## Resource Management

### Hp As Resource

Baalorlord's core teaching: HP is a resource to be SPENT, not hoarded. Taking 5 damage in a hallway fight to end it 1 turn faster is often correct because it saves you from taking 10 damage over 2 additional turns.

#### Key Principles

- HP is a resource, not a score — spending HP efficiently is a skill
- Taking damage to end fights faster is often correct (less total damage taken)
- Low HP forces bad pathing — maintaining 50%+ HP gives you options
- Resting at campfires is almost always wrong if you're above 50% HP — upgrade instead
- Elite fights are worth the HP investment if you can afford it — the rewards are massive

#### Hp Thresholds

**Comfortable:** 70%+ HP — take any fight, hunt elites freely

**Moderate:** 50-70% HP — still take elites if your deck is strong, otherwise play safe

**Danger:** 30-50% HP — avoid elites, consider resting at campfires

**Critical:** Below 30% HP — rest at every campfire, take safest possible path, use potions liberally

### Potion Usage

Baalorlord strongly advocates using potions aggressively, especially on elites. Hoarding potions for the boss is one of the most common mistakes.

#### Key Principles

- Use potions on elites — elite rewards (relics, extra cards, gold) are worth more than saving potions
- A potion used to take 0 damage from an elite is better than saving it for a boss where you'd take 10 damage anyway
- Potions are free power — there is no cost to using them except opportunity cost of a better use later
- You will find more potions — don't hoard them
- If you have 3+ potions going into an elite, use at least 1-2
- The only time to save potions is if you're about to fight a boss and your deck genuinely needs the help

#### Potion Priority

- Use offensive potions (Strength, Fire, Attack potions) on elites to kill them faster
- Use defensive potions (Block, Fairy in a Bottle) when you'd otherwise take lethal or near-lethal damage
- Smoke Bomb is an emergency escape — use it if a fight is going badly and you'd lose 40+ HP
- Entropic Brew / Fruit Juice are best used before tough fights to maximize their value

### Gold Management

Gold is valuable but should be spent strategically. Don't hoard gold — spend it at shops on high-impact purchases.

#### Key Principles

- Card removal is almost always worth the gold — removing a Strike or Defend improves every future fight
- Relics from shops can be game-changing — evaluate them against your deck's needs
- Don't buy cards from shops unless they fill a critical need — card rewards are free
- Save 300-400+ gold for a shop visit for maximum value
- Prioritize: Card Removal > Key Relics > Potions > Cards

#### Shop Priority

- 1. Card removal (always buy at least one removal per shop visit)
- 2. High-synergy relics that complement your deck
- 3. Potions if you're about to fight an elite or boss
- 4. Cards only if they fill a critical gap in your deck
- 5. Colorless cards if they're premium (Apotheosis, Master of Strategy, etc.)

## Act Transitions

What your deck should look like at each stage of the run.

### Act1 Exit

**Deck Size:** 15-20 cards

#### Requirements

- At least 1 scaling source
- Enough frontload to kill hallway enemies in 2-3 turns
- Some block generation beyond starting Defends
- 1-2 card removals completed
- At least 3-4 upgrades

### Act2 Exit

**Deck Size:** 20-25 cards

#### Requirements

- Strong scaling that works reliably
- Good block density (~33%)
- AOE capability for multi-enemy fights
- 50%+ cards upgraded
- Core synergies established

### Act3 Entry

**Focus:** Consolidation and optimization

#### Requirements

- Deck is mostly complete — skip most card rewards
- Focus on upgrades and card removal
- Prepare specifically for the Act 3 boss
- Ensure you have answers for the toughest fights

## Meta Principles

**Adaptability:** Never force a build. Adapt to what the game offers you. The best players build around the cards and relics they find, not the archetype they wanted.

**Information Usage:** Use all available information: upcoming enemies, map layout, boss identity, current HP, potion slots. Every decision should incorporate known information.

**Risk Assessment:** Every decision involves risk. Calculate expected outcomes: 'If I take this elite path, I gain a relic but might lose 20 HP. Is that worth it given my current state?'

**Long Term Thinking:** Don't optimize for the current fight — optimize for the current ACT. A card that's bad now but great for the boss is worth taking if you can survive without it until then.

**Practice Mindset:** Every loss is a learning opportunity. Ask 'What could I have done differently?' after every run. The best players constantly self-evaluate.

# Pathing Strategy

## Look Ahead Method

Baalorlord's fundamental pathing principle: before choosing a path, look at the ENTIRE act map and plan your route from bottom to top. Don't make node-by-node decisions — plan the whole act.

### Steps

- 1. Look at the boss node at the top — identify what boss you're facing and what your deck needs to beat it
- 2. Identify all elite nodes, campfire nodes, shop nodes, and question mark nodes
- 3. Plan a path that hits the right number of elites for your deck strength (usually 2-3 in Act 1)
- 4. Ensure you hit at least 1 campfire before each elite if possible
- 5. Plan shop visits when you'll have 300+ gold
- 6. Prefer paths with more hallway fights early (card rewards to build your deck) and more campfires/shops late (to prepare for the boss)
- 7. Have a backup path in mind if you take more damage than expected

**Key Insight:** The map is deterministic — you can see exactly what's coming. Use this information. Players who path reactively (choosing at each fork) perform significantly worse than those who plan ahead.

## Campfire Strategy

Campfire decisions (rest vs upgrade vs other options) are among the most impactful decisions in any run.

### Rest Vs Upgrade

**General Rule:** Upgrade is almost always correct if you're above 50% HP. The cumulative value of an upgrade over the rest of the run usually exceeds the HP you'd recover.

#### Rest When

- Below 40% HP and you have tough fights ahead (elites, boss)
- You would die to the next fight without healing
- All your key cards are already upgraded
- You have Regal Pillow (rest heals 15 extra HP) making rest more efficient
- The upcoming path is very dangerous and you need the safety margin

#### Upgrade When

- Above 50% HP
- You have a high-impact card to upgrade (key scaling card, important block card)
- You're early in the act and the upgrade will pay dividends over many fights
- You have healing from other sources (Burning Blood, Feed, relics)

### Upgrade Priority

Which card to upgrade at a campfire. Prioritize cards that gain the most from upgrading.

#### Tier 1 Priority

- Cards that gain new effects (e.g., Bash+ applies 3 Vulnerable instead of 2)
- Cards that reduce cost (2-cost becoming 1-cost is massive)
- Key scaling cards (your primary damage/block engine)
- Cards you play every single combat

#### Tier 2 Priority

- Draw cards (more draw = better consistency)
- Block cards you rely on for survival
- AOE cards before multi-enemy fights

#### Tier 3 Priority

- Minor stat increases (+3 damage, +3 block)
- Situational cards you only play occasionally
- Cards that will be removed soon anyway

### Special Campfire Options

**Lift:** Gain 1 Strength permanently. Take this when you have no high-impact upgrade targets. Compounds with multi-hit attacks.

**Toke:** Remove a card (from Girya or other sources). Excellent for removing Strikes/Defends.

**Dig:** Gain a relic (from Shovel). Always take the relic — relics are permanent power.

## Elite Hunting

Elites are the primary way to gain relics, which are permanent power increases. Hunting elites aggressively is key to strong runs, but you need to manage risk.

### Hp Thresholds

#### Act1

**Safe To Fight:** 60%+ HP (48+ HP for most characters)

**Risky:** 40-60% HP — fight only if your deck is strong or you have potions

**Avoid:** Below 40% HP — the relic isn't worth dying

#### Act2

**Safe To Fight:** 50%+ HP (40+ HP for most characters)

**Risky:** 30-50% HP — only with potions and a strong deck

**Avoid:** Below 30% HP

#### Act3

**Safe To Fight:** 50%+ HP with a well-built deck

**Risky:** 30-50% HP — consider your deck's matchup against the specific elite

**Avoid:** Below 30% HP — focus on reaching the boss healthy

### Target Elites Per Act

**Act1:** 2-3 elites. You need relics to snowball your run. 1 elite is too few, 4 is greedy.

**Act2:** 2-3 elites. Continue building relic advantage. Act 2 elites are harder but rewards are proportionally better.

**Act3:** 1-2 elites. Be more selective — you're preparing for the final boss, not building your deck.

### Elite Specific Strategies

#### Byrdonis

Flying enemy that alternates between attacking and buffing. Can stack Strength quickly.

**Key Counter:** Kill fast before Strength stacks become overwhelming. Frontloaded damage is king.

**Danger Level:** Medium — predictable pattern but punishes slow decks

##### Tips

- Apply Weak to reduce its attack damage significantly
- Prioritize damage over block in the first 2 turns
- If it buffs, you have one turn to deal major damage before the buffed attack hits

#### Entomancer

Summons minions that attack independently. Can overwhelm you with multiple damage sources.

**Key Counter:** AOE damage to clear minions. Focus the Entomancer itself when minions are dead.

**Danger Level:** High — multiple damage sources are hard to block against

##### Tips

- AOE is essential — without it, minions will chip you down
- Kill minions first, then focus the Entomancer
- Block is less effective because damage comes from multiple sources
- Potions are very valuable here if you lack AOE

#### Decimillipede

Multi-hitting enemy that benefits from long fights. Applies debuffs and scales over time.

**Key Counter:** End the fight quickly. Scaling damage and strong frontload.

**Danger Level:** Medium-High — gets worse the longer the fight goes

##### Tips

- This is a race — kill it before its scaling overwhelms your block
- Strength and damage scaling are your best friends here
- Artifact can prevent its debuffs from sticking
- Don't try to out-block it long-term; focus on offense

#### Infested Prism

Tanky elite with high HP. May spawn minions or have damage reflection mechanics.

**Key Counter:** Sustained damage output and patience. This is a longer fight.

**Danger Level:** Medium — not as bursty but punishes low-damage decks

##### Tips

- Scaling is very important for this fight due to high enemy HP
- Maintain block consistency throughout the fight
- Poison and other damage-over-time effects are very effective
- Don't rush — this fight rewards steady play

## Shop Timing

Shops are valuable for card removal, relics, and potions. Time your shop visits to maximize gold efficiency.

### Optimal Timing

**Frequency:** Visit ~1 shop per act. More if you have excess gold, fewer if you're gold-starved.

**When To Visit:** Late in the act when you've accumulated gold from fights. Aim to have 300-400+ gold when you hit a shop.

**Avoid:** Don't visit shops with less than 150 gold — you won't be able to afford anything impactful.

### Shop Priorities

#### Always Buy

- Card removal (75-100 gold, increasing per removal) — removing a Strike/Defend improves EVERY future fight
- High-synergy relics that directly complement your deck strategy
- Emergency potions if you're about to fight a tough elite/boss and need help

#### Usually Buy

- Strong colorless cards (Apotheosis, Master of Strategy, Panacea)
- Key missing pieces for your deck (e.g., AOE if you have none)
- Relics with broad utility (energy relics, draw relics)

#### Sometimes Buy

- Cards that fill a secondary need
- Potions for the boss fight
- Situational relics

#### Rarely Buy

- Cards you could get from rewards
- Niche relics with limited application
- Anything when you're low on gold and have more shops ahead

### Gold Earning Tips

- Take gold rewards from fights when you don't need the card or potion
- Question mark events sometimes give gold
- Selling potions at shops if you have excess
- Some relics generate gold passively

## Boss Preparation

Preparing for the act boss is a key part of pathing. You can see which boss you'll face from the start of the act.

### General Approach

- Check the boss icon at the start of each act
- Counter-draft: pick cards that specifically address the boss's mechanics
- Ensure your deck has both damage scaling and block for the boss fight
- Use the last 2-3 fights before the boss to fine-tune (upgrade, remove cards, use events)

### Pre Boss Checklist

- Do I have enough scaling to win a 10+ turn fight?
- Do I have enough block to survive the boss's damage output?
- Do I have an answer for the boss's specific mechanics?
- Am I above 50% HP? If not, should I rest at the next campfire?
- Do I have potions that will help in this specific fight?
- Have I removed enough Strikes/Defends to keep my deck consistent?

## Act By Act Guidance

### Act1

**Theme:** Build Your Deck — Establish your foundation

**Primary Goal:** Get enough cards to beat the Act 1 boss. Focus on frontloaded damage and basic scaling.

#### Pathing Priorities

- Take early hallway fights for card rewards — you need cards to build your deck
- Fight 2-3 elites for relics (relics are permanent power)
- Hit at least 1 campfire for an upgrade before the boss
- Visit a shop if you have 250+ gold (card removal is critical)
- Question marks are fine but hallway fights are often better in Act 1 (guaranteed card rewards)

**Card Taking:** Take cards somewhat liberally in Act 1. You need to fill jobs (damage, block, scaling). Be pickier as you approach the boss.

**Common Act1 Mistake:** Being too greedy with elites. If your deck isn't ready for an elite, the relic isn't worth 40+ HP of damage.

### Act2

**Theme:** Refine Your Deck — Solidify your strategy

**Primary Goal:** Establish your core synergies and scaling. Your deck should have a clear identity by the end of Act 2.

#### Pathing Priorities

- Continue fighting elites (2-3) for relics
- Prioritize campfires for upgrades — upgraded cards scale your power significantly
- Shop visits are important for card removal and key relics
- Start being more selective with card rewards — skip anything that doesn't fit your strategy
- Question marks can provide valuable events (card transforms, relics, etc.)

**Card Taking:** Be much pickier than Act 1. Only take cards that directly strengthen your core strategy or fill a critical weakness.

**Common Act2 Mistake:** Taking too many cards. Your deck should be 20-25 cards by end of Act 2. Every card you add increases cycle time.

### Act3

**Theme:** Consolidate — Prepare for the final boss

**Primary Goal:** Optimize your existing deck through upgrades and removals. Skip most card rewards.

#### Pathing Priorities

- Fight 1-2 elites if you're healthy and your deck handles them well
- Campfires for upgrades are very valuable — every upgrade matters for the final boss
- Final shop visit for last-chance card removal or critical purchases
- Avoid unnecessary damage — reaching the boss healthy is paramount
- Plan your path to the boss with maximum campfires and minimum risk

**Card Taking:** Skip 60%+ of card rewards. Your deck is built — focus on making it better, not bigger.

**Common Act3 Mistake:** Still taking cards. Your deck is nearly complete. Adding more cards dilutes your best cards.

## Risk Management

How to assess and manage risk during pathing decisions.

### Risk Factors

- Current HP percentage — lower HP = higher risk
- Deck strength — stronger decks can handle riskier paths
- Available potions — potions provide a safety net for tough fights
- Upcoming nodes — know what's coming before you commit to a path
- Act progression — more risk is acceptable early in an act, less acceptable near the boss

### Risk Mitigation

- Always have a backup path planned
- Keep potions for emergencies (but don't hoard them — use on elites)
- Rest at campfires when below 40% HP with tough fights ahead
- Take safer paths when your deck has clear weaknesses
- Smoke Bomb potion is an emergency escape from a fight going badly

### Hp Threshold Guidance

**Above 70:** Play aggressively — hunt elites, take risks, upgrade at campfires

**50 To 70:** Play normally — take elites if your deck is ready, upgrade when safe

**30 To 50:** Play carefully — avoid elites without potions, consider resting

**Below 30:** Play defensively — rest at every campfire, take the safest path, use potions liberally

## Question Mark Strategy

Question mark nodes (unknown events) can provide card transforms, relics, gold, healing, card removal, or sometimes negative effects.

### When To Prioritize

- When you need healing but don't want to waste a campfire resting
- When you're looking for card transforms or unusual options
- When hallway fights aren't giving you useful card rewards
- When you have relics that benefit from events (e.g., Ssserpent Head)

### When To Avoid

- When you desperately need specific card rewards (hallway fights are more reliable)
- When you can't afford any negative event outcomes
- When you need guaranteed combat encounters for gold or card rewards

### Tips

- Many events are beneficial — don't fear question marks
- Some events offer free card removal, which is extremely valuable
- Events that offer max HP increases are almost always worth taking
- Card transform events can turn bad cards into great ones (or vice versa — risk/reward)

# Common Mistakes

## Mistakes

### Card Bloat

Taking too many cards, resulting in a bloated deck with inconsistent draws. The player adds cards without considering the impact on cycle time and draw consistency. Deck becomes unfocused — the player has many 'okay' cards but rarely sees their best cards when they need them.

**Severity:** high

**Frequency:** very_common

#### Why It Happens

- New players feel that more cards = more power, when the opposite is often true
- Fear of skipping — players feel they're 'wasting' a card reward by not taking anything
- Not understanding cycle time — players don't realize that a 35-card deck sees key cards half as often as a 20-card deck
- Taking cards 'just in case' without a specific plan for when they'll be useful
- Evaluating cards in isolation rather than in the context of the whole deck
- Excitement over seemingly powerful cards without considering if they fit the deck's strategy

#### How To Fix

- Before every card reward, ask: 'Does this card make my deck better, or just bigger?'
- Track your deck size — aim for 20-25 cards by end of Act 2
- Skip card rewards more often — skipping 40-60% of rewards in Act 2+ is normal for strong players
- Prioritize card removal at shops to offset cards you've taken
- Use the 'Jobs Framework' — only take cards that fill a specific, unfilled role in your deck
- Review your deck regularly and ask: 'Which cards do I wish I wasn't drawing?'

#### Detection Criteria

##### Deck Size Thresholds

**Act1 Warning:** More than 22 cards by end of Act 1

**Act2 Warning:** More than 28 cards by end of Act 2

**Act3 Warning:** More than 32 cards by end of Act 3

##### Behavioral Signs

- Player takes a card from almost every reward (>80% take rate)
- Player has multiple cards serving the same role (redundant cards)
- Player rarely or never skips card rewards
- Player has cards that were never or rarely played in recent combats
- Deck has both aggressive and defensive scaling that don't synergize

##### Combat Signs

- Player frequently doesn't draw their key cards when needed
- Fights take longer than necessary because draws are inconsistent
- Player has leftover energy but bad cards to play (hand is full of mediocre options)

#### Coaching Response

**Immediate:** Point out the deck size relative to the act. Compare their take rate to recommended rates.

**Educational:** Explain cycle time: 'Your deck has 30 cards. With a 5-card hand, it takes 6 draws (3 turns) to see your whole deck. If your key combo is 3 cards, you might not see it for 4+ turns.'

**Actionable:** Recommend skipping the current card reward unless one card fills a critical need. Suggest card removal at the next shop.


### Forcing Archetypes Early

Committing to a specific build (e.g., 'I'm going Poison Silent' or 'I'm doing Strength Ironclad') before seeing what the game offers. This causes players to pass on strong cards that don't fit their preconceived plan and take weak cards that do.

**Severity:** high

**Frequency:** common

#### Why It Happens

- Players watch streamers pilot specific archetypes and want to replicate them
- Deck-building games encourage 'theme' thinking — players want a cohesive identity early
- It feels good to have a plan — uncertainty is uncomfortable
- Players remember their best runs with a specific archetype and try to recreate them
- Confusion between 'having a direction' (good) and 'forcing an archetype' (bad)
- Not understanding that strong decks are built from what you're offered, not what you want

#### How To Fix

- Stay flexible through Act 1 — take the best card offered regardless of archetype
- Let your deck's identity emerge from the cards and relics you find
- Evaluate each card reward independently: 'Is this the best card for my deck RIGHT NOW?'
- Don't commit to an archetype until you have 3-4 strong cards in that direction
- Remember that hybrid decks are often stronger than 'pure' archetype decks
- Focus on the Four Pillars (damage, cycle, block, upgrades) rather than archetypes

#### Detection Criteria

##### Behavioral Signs

- Player passes on strong general-purpose cards in favor of weak archetype-specific cards
- Player states their build plan in Act 1 ('I'm going Shiv build')
- Player takes archetype cards that don't work without other archetype pieces they don't have yet
- Player ignores the Four Pillars in favor of archetype synergy
- Player is disappointed by card rewards that don't match their desired archetype

##### Deck Signs

- Deck has archetype-specific cards but lacks the support cards to make them work
- Deck is missing basic needs (block, frontload damage) because player skipped non-archetype cards
- Deck has clear archetype identity but performs poorly because key pieces are missing

#### Coaching Response

**Immediate:** Ask the player why they're passing on the strong card. Challenge archetype-based reasoning.

**Educational:** Explain adaptability: 'The best STS2 players build around what the game gives them. If the game offers you 3 strong Poison cards, go Poison. If it offers you 3 strong Shiv cards, go Shiv. Don't decide in advance.'

**Actionable:** Recommend the strongest card in the current reward regardless of archetype. Point out how it fills a job the deck needs.


### Ignoring Pathing Strategy

Not planning map routes in advance. The player makes node-by-node decisions instead of planning the entire act's path. This leads to suboptimal routes — missing elites when strong, hitting elites when weak, visiting shops with no gold, or skipping campfires before tough fights.

**Severity:** high

**Frequency:** common

#### Why It Happens

- Players focus on the immediate decision ('left or right?') instead of the big picture
- Map information feels overwhelming — too many variables to process
- Players don't realize they can see the full map and plan ahead
- Reactive play is easier than proactive planning
- Not understanding which node types are most valuable at different points in the run
- Lack of awareness of the Look Ahead Method

#### How To Fix

- Use the Look Ahead Method: plan your entire act path from bottom to top before taking your first step
- Identify the boss first — know what you're building toward
- Count elites, campfires, shops, and question marks on each possible route
- Consider your HP, deck state, and gold when choosing between routes
- Have a backup path if things go wrong (take more damage than expected, etc.)
- Re-evaluate your path at every decision point — adjust if your situation has changed

#### Detection Criteria

##### Behavioral Signs

- Player doesn't examine the full map before making pathing decisions
- Player makes pathing decisions quickly without analysis
- Player hits shops with less than 150 gold
- Player enters elite fights at low HP (below 40%)
- Player skips campfires before tough fights when they need healing or upgrades
- Player doesn't consider the boss when making pathing choices

##### Outcome Signs

- Player arrives at boss with suboptimal HP or deck state
- Player misses elite opportunities when they were strong enough to fight
- Player visits shops without enough gold for meaningful purchases
- Player reaches campfires with no good upgrade targets (already upgraded key cards earlier)

#### Coaching Response

**Immediate:** Before the player moves to the next node, suggest they look at the full map and plan their route.

**Educational:** Explain the Look Ahead Method step by step. Show how planning ahead leads to better outcomes.

**Actionable:** Provide a recommended path for the current act with reasoning for each node.


### Playing on Autopilot

Going through the motions without thinking through individual turns. Playing cards in the same order every fight, not considering enemy intent, not doing damage/block math. This leads to suboptimal plays that compound over a run.

**Severity:** medium

**Frequency:** very_common

#### Why It Happens

- Fights become repetitive and players stop thinking critically
- Players develop habits ('always play Strikes first, then Defends') without evaluating each turn
- Fatigue during long runs — mental energy decreases as the run progresses
- Overconfidence in easy fights — players don't bother optimizing 'simple' encounters
- Not understanding that small optimizations compound over many fights
- Lack of awareness of enemy intent indicators and how to play around them

#### How To Fix

- Check enemy intent EVERY turn before playing any cards
- Do the math: calculate exactly how much damage you need to deal and how much block you need
- Consider card order — some cards benefit from being played before others (Vulnerable before attacks)
- Ask 'What's the worst that can happen this turn?' before committing to plays
- Identify lethal threats — know when the enemy can kill you and plan accordingly
- Take short breaks during long runs to maintain focus

#### Detection Criteria

##### Behavioral Signs

- Player plays cards in the same order every turn regardless of enemy intent
- Player doesn't check enemy intent indicators
- Player doesn't calculate damage/block math for the turn
- Player makes plays quickly without pausing to think
- Player ends turn with unspent energy and playable cards
- Player doesn't adjust strategy based on enemy behavior changes

##### Outcome Signs

- Player takes unnecessary damage from predictable enemy attacks
- Player over-blocks (wastes block) or under-blocks (takes preventable damage)
- Player kills enemies one turn later than necessary due to suboptimal play order
- Player misses lethal on enemies, extending fights unnecessarily

#### Coaching Response

**Immediate:** Ask the player to pause and check enemy intent before making plays.

**Educational:** Show specific examples of how play order and math optimization would have saved HP or ended fights faster.

**Actionable:** Provide a step-by-step analysis of the optimal play for the current turn, showing the reasoning.


### Hoarding Potions

Saving potions 'for the boss' instead of using them on elites and tough hallway fights. This is one of Baalorlord's most-discussed mistakes. Potions used on elites often save more HP than they would on the boss, and you'll likely find more potions before the boss anyway.

**Severity:** medium

**Frequency:** very_common

#### Why It Happens

- Boss fights feel like the 'big' fight, so players save their best resources for them
- Fear of not having potions when they 'really' need them
- Not understanding that elite fights are often harder relative to your deck than boss fights
- Not tracking potion acquisition — players don't realize how frequently potions drop
- Overvaluing the potion itself vs the HP it saves — using a potion to save 15 HP from an elite is massive value
- Treating potions as 'emergency' items rather than 'efficiency' items

#### How To Fix

- Reframe potions as 'free power' — they cost you nothing to use except the opportunity to use them later
- Use offensive potions on elites to kill them faster and take less damage overall
- Use defensive potions to prevent big damage spikes that would force you to rest instead of upgrade
- If you have 3+ potions, use at least 1-2 on the next elite fight
- Only save potions for the boss if you're 2-3 fights away from it AND your deck needs help
- Track your potion acquisition — you find ~3-5 potions per act

#### Detection Criteria

##### Behavioral Signs

- Player has full potion slots for extended periods (5+ fights)
- Player has 3 potions going into an elite fight and uses none
- Player takes significant damage from elites while holding offensive potions
- Player states they're 'saving potions for the boss'
- Player discards potions at fights to make room for new ones (shows they weren't using them)
- Player has defensive potions while low on HP but doesn't use them preemptively

##### Outcome Signs

- Player arrives at the boss with full potions but has lost significant HP along the way
- Player had to rest at campfires instead of upgrading because they took too much damage from elites they could have used potions on
- Player's deck is weaker than it should be because they skipped elites they could have beaten with potion help

#### Coaching Response

**Immediate:** Suggest using a specific potion in the current fight. Explain the HP value it would save.

**Educational:** Show the math: 'If you use this Strength potion on this elite, you kill it 1 turn faster, saving ~15 HP. That's worth more than saving the potion for a boss where it might save 5 HP.'

**Actionable:** Before each elite fight, suggest which potions to use. After elite fights, note how much HP was saved or could have been saved.


### Misunderstanding Card Value

Evaluating cards incorrectly — often dismissing 2-cost cards as 'too expensive,' evaluating cards in a vacuum instead of deck context, or overvaluing cards that are flashy but don't fill a needed role. Also includes overvaluing rares and undervaluing strong commons/uncommons.

**Severity:** medium

**Frequency:** common

#### Why It Happens

- Players compare raw numbers without considering action efficiency (2-cost card = 1 draw, 2 one-cost cards = 2 draws)
- Players evaluate cards in isolation instead of considering deck context and synergies
- Players gravitate toward 'exciting' cards (rares, flashy effects) over 'boring but effective' cards
- Unfamiliarity with which cards are actually strong in practice vs theory
- Not understanding that a card's value depends heavily on what the deck already has
- Overvaluing card rarity — a strong common is often better than a weak rare

#### How To Fix

- Evaluate 2-cost cards by their total effect AND their draw efficiency (1 card slot instead of 2)
- Always evaluate cards in the context of your current deck: 'Does my deck need what this card does?'
- Prefer cards that fill multiple roles (damage + block, damage + draw, block + draw)
- Don't be swayed by rarity — a Shrug It Off (common) is often better than a mediocre rare
- Use the Jobs Framework: identify your deck's needs first, then evaluate which card best fills them
- Consider the card over the entire run — a card you'll play 50 times has 50x its per-play value

#### Detection Criteria

##### Behavioral Signs

- Player consistently skips 2-cost cards in favor of weaker 1-cost alternatives
- Player takes rare cards that don't fit their deck over strong commons/uncommons that do
- Player evaluates cards by raw numbers ('this only does 8 damage') without context
- Player doesn't consider deck needs when choosing cards — takes the 'best card' instead of the 'best card for their deck'
- Player dismisses cards as 'bad' without considering their upgraded versions or synergies

##### Deck Signs

- Deck has many weak 1-cost cards instead of fewer powerful 2-cost cards
- Deck has flashy rares that don't synergize with the rest of the deck
- Deck is missing strong common/uncommon cards that would shore up weaknesses

#### Coaching Response

**Immediate:** When a 2-cost card is offered, show the math: total effect per card slot, draw efficiency, and how it compares to playing two 1-cost cards.

**Educational:** Explain the 'card slot' concept: 'Every card in your hand takes one draw to get there. A 2-cost card that does the work of two 1-cost cards is effectively giving you a free draw.'

**Actionable:** Recommend cards based on deck needs, not card rarity or raw numbers. Show how the recommended card fills a specific job.


## Meta Detection

How the coaching engine should prioritize mistake detection and feedback.

### Priority Order

- card_bloat — check deck size against act thresholds and take rate
- hoarding_potions — check potion slot usage and elite fight behavior
- ignoring_pathing — check if player is using Look Ahead Method
- autopilot — check for enemy intent awareness and play optimization
- forcing_archetypes — check for rigid card selection patterns
- misunderstanding_card_value — check for 2-cost card avoidance and context-free evaluation

**Feedback Frequency:** Don't overwhelm the player. Focus on 1-2 mistakes per act. Address the most impactful mistake first.

**Feedback Tone:** Constructive and educational, never condescending. Frame feedback as 'here's how to improve' rather than 'you did this wrong.'

**Positive Reinforcement:** When the player makes a correct decision that avoids a common mistake, acknowledge it. 'Good skip — your deck doesn't need another attack card right now.'

# Mechanics

## Character Mechanics

### Sly

When a card with Sly is discarded from your hand (not played, not exhausted — specifically discarded), it is automatically played for free. This creates powerful synergies with discard effects.

**Character:** Silent

**Type:** keyword_mechanic

#### How It Works

- Cards with the Sly keyword sit in your hand like normal cards
- If any effect causes you to discard them (Acrobatics, Survivor, Gamble, etc.), they trigger automatically
- The Sly card is played for free — no energy cost
- Sly triggers BEFORE the discard resolves, so draw effects from Sly cards happen immediately
- Multiple Sly cards in hand will all trigger if you discard them simultaneously

#### Key Synergies

- Acrobatics — draw 3, discard 1. Discarding a Sly card means you draw 3 AND play a free card
- Survivor — discard 1, gain block. Discarding a Sly card gives you block AND a free card play
- Gamble — discard hand, draw equal. All Sly cards trigger before redraw
- Calculated Gamble — upgraded, doesn't lose Sly cards on discard
- Any card or relic that causes discarding from hand

#### Strategic Tips

- Build decks around forced discard effects to trigger Sly consistently
- Sly attacks get full damage when triggered — they're essentially free damage
- Sly block cards provide free block — excellent for defensive consistency
- Having too many Sly cards without enough discard triggers leads to dead draws
- Sly + draw effects = massive hand cycling and card advantage

#### Common Mistakes

- Playing Sly cards normally instead of setting up discard triggers — you lose the free play
- Not having enough discard effects to reliably trigger Sly cards
- Taking too many Sly cards without considering discard density

### Forge

Forge is a persistent counter that increases the damage of Sovereign Blade. Each point of Forge adds damage to every Sovereign Blade strike. Forge persists across turns within a combat but resets between combats (unless modified by specific relics).

**Character:** Regent

**Type:** scaling_mechanic

#### How It Works

- Forge stacks are accumulated through specific cards and effects
- Each Forge stack increases the damage of Sovereign Blade attacks
- Forge is the Regent's primary damage scaling mechanic
- Stacks persist within a combat — building Forge early pays dividends in long fights
- Some relics can preserve Forge stacks between combats

#### Key Synergies

- Sovereign Blade — the primary beneficiary of Forge stacks
- Cards that generate Forge quickly — look for multi-Forge generation
- Cards that let you play Sovereign Blade multiple times per turn
- Relics that add Forge at combat start or passively

#### Strategic Tips

- Forge is exponential scaling — invest early in Forge generation for big payoffs in long fights
- Boss fights are where Forge shines — the longer the fight, the more value your Forge investment provides
- Balance Forge generation with immediate survival — you need to live long enough for Forge to matter
- Sovereign Blade's base damage plus Forge can reach extremely high numbers in long fights

### Doom

Doom is a death mark applied to enemies. If an enemy's Doom value is greater than or equal to their current HP at the end of their turn, they are instantly killed. Doom does not deal damage — it triggers an instant kill threshold check.

**Character:** Necrobinder

**Type:** debuff_mechanic

#### How It Works

- Doom stacks are applied to enemies through Necrobinder cards and effects
- At the end of the enemy's turn, a check occurs: if Doom >= enemy's current HP, the enemy dies instantly
- Doom does NOT deal damage directly — it's a kill threshold
- Doom stacks persist on the enemy (they don't decrease automatically unless specified)
- Multiple Doom applications stack additively
- Doom works on most enemies but may be resisted by certain bosses or have limited effect on high-HP targets

#### Key Synergies

- Damage cards that lower enemy HP to meet the Doom threshold
- Cards that apply large amounts of Doom quickly
- Multi-target Doom application for AOE encounters
- Cards that apply Doom AND deal damage simultaneously

#### Strategic Tips

- Doom is most effective against enemies with moderate HP — it instant-kills when HP drops below Doom
- Combine Doom with direct damage: apply Doom, then deal enough damage to push HP below the Doom threshold
- In multi-enemy fights, spreading Doom can help clear enemies efficiently
- Against bosses with high HP, Doom requires significant investment — consider if direct damage is more efficient
- Doom essentially means you don't need to deal the last X points of damage, where X = Doom applied
- Think of Doom as 'the enemy has X fewer effective HP'

#### Common Mistakes

- Applying Doom without dealing damage — Doom alone doesn't kill until HP drops below it
- Over-investing in Doom against low-HP enemies that would die to regular attacks anyway
- Not understanding the timing — Doom checks at END of enemy turn, not start

### Stars

Stars are a persistent secondary resource for the Regent. Stars are generated by specific cards and effects, and can be spent to power up other cards or abilities. Stars persist across turns within combat.

**Character:** Regent

**Type:** resource_mechanic

#### How It Works

- Stars are generated by playing specific Regent cards or using certain abilities
- Stars are spent (consumed) when playing cards that require Stars as a cost or benefit from Stars
- Stars persist within a combat — unspent Stars carry over between turns
- Some effects scale with the number of Stars you have (without consuming them)
- Stars do NOT carry over between combats (unless modified by specific relics)

#### Key Synergies

- Star-generating cards — your 'engine' cards that build up Stars
- Star-consuming cards — powerful effects that spend Stars for big impact
- Star-scaling cards — effects that grow stronger based on current Star count
- Relics that generate Stars passively or at combat start

#### Strategic Tips

- Build a balance of Star generators and Star consumers — too many of one without the other is wasteful
- In long fights, generate Stars early and spend them on powerful turns
- Star management is like energy management — plan your Star budget across turns
- Some cards generate Stars as a side effect — these are valuable because they provide Stars without dedicating a card play
- Don't hoard Stars forever — spend them for big impact turns

### Souls

Souls are special zero-cost skill cards unique to the Necrobinder. When played, they draw 2 cards and then exhaust (are removed from the deck for the rest of combat). They provide free card cycling but are consumable within each fight.

**Character:** Necrobinder

**Type:** card_mechanic

#### How It Works

- Souls cost 0 energy to play
- When played, Souls draw 2 cards immediately
- After being played, Souls exhaust — they are removed from the deck for the rest of combat
- Souls are shuffled back into your deck at the start of each new combat
- New Souls can be generated during combat through specific Necrobinder effects

#### Key Synergies

- Exhaust synergies — cards that trigger when other cards are exhausted
- Card draw chains — Souls drawing into more Souls creates explosive draw turns
- Necrobinder cards that generate additional Souls during combat
- Effects that benefit from high card throughput (playing many cards per turn)

#### Strategic Tips

- Souls are excellent for finding your key cards faster — free draw 2 with deck thinning
- In long fights, Souls exhaust early, thinning your deck and making remaining draws more consistent
- Generating Souls during combat extends your card advantage and keeps your cycling strong
- Souls are at their best in the first few turns — they help you set up your engine quickly
- Don't hold Souls in hand — play them immediately to start cycling
- Exhaust-based strategies love Souls — each Soul exhausted triggers exhaust benefits

### Osty

Osty is the Necrobinder's undead companion, auto-summoned at the start of each combat. Osty acts as both an attacker and a shield, absorbing enemy attacks directed at it. Managing Osty is central to Necrobinder strategy.

**Character:** Necrobinder

**Type:** companion_mechanic

#### How It Works

- Osty is automatically summoned at the start of every combat
- Osty has its own HP pool and can take damage from enemy attacks
- Enemies may target Osty instead of you, effectively making Osty a meat shield
- Specific Necrobinder cards command Osty to attack, defend, or use special abilities
- If Osty dies during combat, certain effects can resummon it
- Osty's HP and abilities can be enhanced through specific cards and relics

#### Strategic Tips

- Use Osty as a damage sponge — enemies attacking Osty are not attacking you
- Keep Osty alive in tough fights to maintain your defensive buffer
- Some builds focus on empowering Osty's attacks for significant damage output
- Don't neglect your own block just because Osty can take hits — some enemies target you directly
- Osty dying is not the end of the world — some cards benefit from Osty being resummoned

## Enchantments And Afflictions

### Enchantments

Enchantments are permanent positive modifications applied to cards. They come from specific events, relics, or encounters. Once enchanted, a card keeps its enchantment for the rest of the run.

**Type:** card_modifier

#### How They Work

- Enchantments are applied to specific cards in your deck
- They add positive effects to the card (reduced cost, added damage, extra draw, etc.)
- Enchantments persist for the entire run — they're permanent power increases
- A single card can potentially have multiple enchantments
- Enchantments are separate from upgrades — a card can be both upgraded AND enchanted

#### Common Enchantments

- Cost reduction — the enchanted card costs less energy
- Added damage — the enchanted card deals extra damage
- Added block — the enchanted card provides extra block
- Draw on play — the enchanted card draws additional cards when played
- Retain — the enchanted card retains in your hand between turns

#### Strategic Tips

- Enchant your most-played cards for maximum value over the run
- Cost reduction enchantments on 2-cost cards are incredibly powerful
- Draw enchantments on cards you play every turn provide consistent extra cycling
- Some events let you choose which card to enchant — pick your strongest, most-played card

### Afflictions

Afflictions are negative modifications applied to your cards by enemies or events. They weaken the affected card until the affliction is removed.

**Type:** negative_card_modifier

#### How They Work

- Afflictions are applied to specific cards in your deck by enemy effects or events
- They add negative effects (increased cost, reduced damage, debuffs when played, etc.)
- Some afflictions are permanent, others are temporary (lasting one combat or one act)
- Afflictions can be removed through specific events, relics, or card effects
- Playing an afflicted card triggers the negative effect in addition to the card's normal effect

#### Common Afflictions

- Increased cost — the afflicted card costs more energy
- Reduced damage — the afflicted card deals less damage
- Self-damage — playing the afflicted card damages you
- Debuff on play — playing the afflicted card applies a debuff to you

#### Strategic Tips

- Prioritize removing afflictions from your key cards — afflicted key cards hurt your whole run
- If a card has a serious affliction, consider removing the card entirely at a shop
- Some afflictions are minor enough to ignore — evaluate the impact before spending resources to remove them
- Exhaust-based strategies can work around afflictions by exhausting the afflicted card out of rotation

## Orbs

Orbs are the Defect's signature mechanic. The Defect channels orbs into orb slots, where they provide passive effects each turn and powerful evoke effects when triggered.

**Character:** Defect

**Type:** channeling_mechanic

### Orb Types

#### Lightning

**Name:** Lightning

**Passive Effect:** Deals 3 damage to a random enemy at end of turn

**Evoke Effect:** Deals 8 damage to a random enemy immediately

**Scaling:** Focus increases both passive and evoke damage

**Strategic Use:** Primary damage orb. Channel multiple Lightning orbs for consistent damage each turn.

##### Tips

- Lightning passive damage adds up quickly with multiple orbs
- Focus scaling makes Lightning orbs increasingly powerful
- Random targeting can be a downside in multi-enemy fights — you can't choose the target
- Electrodynamics makes Lightning hit ALL enemies, solving the targeting issue

#### Frost

**Name:** Frost

**Passive Effect:** Generates 2 block at end of turn

**Evoke Effect:** Generates 5 block immediately

**Scaling:** Focus increases both passive and evoke block

**Strategic Use:** Primary defensive orb. Channel Frost orbs for consistent block generation.

##### Tips

- Frost orbs with high Focus can generate enough block to survive almost anything
- Multiple Frost orbs provide stacking block — the more you have, the safer you are
- Frost + Focus is the Defect's primary defensive scaling engine
- Frost orbs are excellent for long boss fights where sustained block is critical

#### Dark

**Name:** Dark

**Passive Effect:** Gains 6 damage at end of turn (stored within the orb, accumulating)

**Evoke Effect:** Deals ALL stored damage to the enemy with lowest HP

**Scaling:** Focus increases the passive damage gain per turn. Stored damage can grow very large.

**Strategic Use:** Burst damage orb. Let it charge up, then evoke for massive damage.

##### Tips

- Dark orbs are the Defect's primary burst damage source
- The longer a Dark orb stays channeled, the more damage it stores
- Evoking a fully-charged Dark orb can deal 50+ damage in a single hit
- Focus increases the charge rate, making Dark orbs scale extremely well
- Pair with cards that evoke orbs on demand to time your Dark orb burst

#### Glass

**Name:** Glass

**Passive Effect:** Varies by the Glass orb type — Glass orbs can have different effects

**Evoke Effect:** Varies — Glass orbs break (shatter) when evoked, applying their unique effect

**Scaling:** Focus may or may not affect Glass orbs depending on the specific type

**Strategic Use:** Utility orbs with unique one-time effects. Use them for specific tactical advantages.

##### Tips

- Glass orbs are situational — evaluate each one based on the current fight
- Some Glass orbs have very powerful evoke effects worth building around
- Glass orbs add variety to the Defect's orb toolkit beyond the core three types

### Orb Mechanics

#### Channeling

Playing orb-generating cards channels orbs into your orb slots. Orbs fill slots from left to right.

##### Rules

- You start with 3 orb slots (can be increased by cards and relics)
- Channeling an orb when all slots are full evokes the leftmost orb
- The leftmost orb is always the first to be evoked
- Channel order matters — put orbs you want to keep in later slots

#### Evoking

Evoking an orb triggers its powerful evoke effect and removes it from its slot.

##### Rules

- Evoking triggers the orb's evoke effect immediately
- The evoked orb is removed from its slot
- Cards that say 'Evoke' specifically trigger evoke effects
- Channeling when full forces an evoke of the leftmost orb

#### Focus

Focus is a buff that enhances all orb passive and evoke effects. Each point of Focus adds to the numerical values of your orbs.

##### Rules

- Focus applies to ALL orbs simultaneously — it's universal orb scaling
- Each point of Focus adds +1 to passive and evoke values
- Focus can be negative (from Biased Cognition's downside), reducing orb effectiveness
- Focus is the single most important stat for orb-based strategies

##### Key Cards

- Defragment — gain 1 Focus permanently
- Biased Cognition — gain 4 Focus, lose 1 Focus per turn
- Consume — remove an orb, gain 2 Focus
- Core Surge — gain Focus and Artifact

## Standard Keywords

### Exhaust

When a card is exhausted, it is removed from your deck for the rest of combat. It goes to the exhaust pile and cannot be drawn again.

#### Strategic Notes

- Exhaust naturally thins your deck during combat, improving cycle time
- Some cards and relics trigger effects when other cards are exhausted
- Exhausting bad cards (Strikes, Defends, Statuses) is always good
- Exhaust-focused strategies use exhaust synergies as a core mechanic
- Dead Branch creates a random card whenever you exhaust a card — powerful with exhaust strategies

### Ethereal

If an Ethereal card is in your hand at the end of your turn and you haven't played it, it is exhausted automatically. Use it or lose it.

#### Strategic Notes

- Ethereal cards force you to play them or lose them — they can't be saved for later
- This makes Ethereal cards less flexible but often more powerful per play
- Retain effects can override Ethereal — a Retained Ethereal card stays in hand
- Plan your turn around Ethereal cards — play them before they auto-exhaust

### Retain

A Retained card stays in your hand between turns instead of being discarded to the draw pile. You keep it in your next hand.

#### Strategic Notes

- Retain lets you save key cards for the perfect turn to play them
- Retained cards don't count toward your next turn's draw — you draw fewer new cards
- Retain is excellent for setup combos — hold a finisher until your scaling is ready
- Some cards gain Retain when upgraded, significantly increasing their flexibility

### Innate

Innate cards are always drawn in your opening hand at the start of combat. They guarantee you have access to specific cards from turn 1.

#### Strategic Notes

- Innate cards improve your turn 1 consistency dramatically
- If you have more Innate cards than your hand size, extras go to the top of your draw pile
- Innate is especially valuable on scaling cards — start scaling immediately
- Cards that gain Innate when upgraded (like Burning Pact+) become significantly better

### Vulnerable

A debuff that causes the target to take 50% more damage from attacks. Duration is measured in turns.

#### Strategic Notes

- Vulnerable is one of the strongest debuffs in the game — 50% more damage is massive
- Apply Vulnerable before attacking for maximum value
- Cards that apply Vulnerable are high priority in card rewards
- Vulnerable doesn't affect non-attack damage (poison, orb damage, etc.)

### Weak

A debuff that causes the target to deal 25% less damage with attacks. When applied to enemies, it reduces incoming damage.

#### Strategic Notes

- Weak is the best defensive debuff — reducing ALL attack damage by 25% is incredibly efficient
- Weak stacks in duration, not intensity — more Weak = longer protection
- Apply Weak to enemies before they attack for maximum HP saved
- Cards that apply Weak are always valuable — Neutralize, Uppercut, etc.

### Strength

A buff that increases attack damage. Each point of Strength adds +1 damage to EVERY attack played, including multi-hit attacks (each hit gets +1).

#### Strategic Notes

- Strength is multiplicative with multi-hit attacks — Heavy Blade with Strength is devastating
- Permanent Strength sources (Demon Form, Inflame) are premium scaling
- Temporary Strength (from potions, Limit Break) is still very valuable for burst turns
- Enemies can also gain Strength — watch for enemy Strength scaling in long fights

### Dexterity

A buff that increases block from block cards. Each point of Dexterity adds +1 block to EVERY block card played.

#### Strategic Notes

- Dexterity is the block equivalent of Strength — it scales all block cards
- Multiple cheap block cards benefit most from Dexterity
- Footwork (Silent) is the primary Dexterity source — very high priority card
- Dexterity makes even basic Defend cards produce meaningful block

### Intangible

While Intangible, ALL damage taken is reduced to 1. This includes attacks, orbs, poison, everything. Extremely powerful but rare.

#### Strategic Notes

- Intangible is the strongest defensive effect in the game
- It makes even the biggest enemy attacks deal only 1 damage
- Wraith Form (Silent) grants Intangible but applies Dexterity loss — must be managed
- Use Intangible turns to set up your offense rather than blocking

### Artifact

A buff that negates the next debuff applied to you. Each stack of Artifact prevents one debuff application.

#### Strategic Notes

- Artifact prevents debuffs from sticking — Weak, Vulnerable, Frail, etc.
- Extremely valuable against enemies that rely on debuffs
- Artifact can negate your OWN debuffs (Biased Cognition's Focus loss, Wraith Form's Dexterity loss)
- Using Artifact to block self-inflicted debuffs is a key advanced strategy

### Frail

A debuff that reduces your block from block cards by 25%. When applied to you, your block cards generate less block.

#### Strategic Notes

- Frail makes your defensive cards less effective — plan accordingly
- Artifact can prevent Frail from being applied
- Non-card block sources (orbs, relics) are NOT affected by Frail
- Frail is especially dangerous when combined with enemy Strength scaling

# Character — Ironclad

**Character:** Ironclad

**Color:** Red

## Identity

The Ironclad is an aggressive, front-line warrior who excels at Strength scaling, Exhaust synergies, and self-sustain through HP recovery. The Ironclad's playstyle rewards aggressive play — killing enemies fast and healing the damage taken. The Ironclad punishes enemies who don't die quickly and has the tools to scale damage to absurd heights.

**Playstyle:** Aggressive with built-in sustain. The Ironclad wants to hit hard, scale Strength, and use exhaust mechanics to thin the deck and trigger powerful synergies. The starting relic (Burning Blood) encourages taking fights because you heal after every combat.

### Strengths

- Best Strength scaling in the game — can reach very high damage numbers
- Strong exhaust synergies that simultaneously thin the deck and generate value
- Built-in sustain through Burning Blood and HP-recovery cards
- Excellent frontloaded damage — can end hallway fights quickly
- Access to Barricade for infinite block retention

### Weaknesses

- Block cards are generally weaker than Silent or Defect — relies on killing fast rather than blocking forever
- Exhaust strategies can run out of cards if not managed carefully
- Vulnerable to fights that punish aggression (enemies that punish attacking, or scale faster than you)
- Some key cards are expensive (2-3 cost) requiring energy management

## Starting Deck

### Strikes

**Count:** 5

**Damage:** 6

**Cost:** 1

**Note:** Remove these as quickly as possible

### Defends

**Count:** 4

**Block:** 5

**Cost:** 1

**Note:** Remove after Strikes

### Bash

**Count:** 1

**Damage:** 8

**Cost:** 2

**Effect:** Apply 2 Vulnerable

**Note:** Upgrade priority — Bash+ applies 3 Vulnerable, massive damage increase

## Starting Relic

**Name:** Burning Blood

**Effect:** Heal 6 HP at the end of combat

**Strategic Value:** Enables aggressive play. The 6 HP healing means you can take more damage in fights and still be healthy for the next fight. This encourages fighting more enemies and hunting elites.

### Tips

- Burning Blood makes upgrading at campfires more attractive — you have passive healing already
- The 6 HP adds up: over 15 fights in an act, that's 90 HP healed passively
- Don't rely on it exclusively — it won't save you from big hits
- It's most valuable in Act 1 where individual fight damage tends to be lower

## Archetypes

### Strength Scaling

The quintessential Ironclad strategy. Stack Strength through permanent buffs and turn every attack into a devastating blow. Multi-hit attacks become especially powerful with Strength.

#### Core Cards

- Demon Form — gain 2/3 Strength per turn. The best Strength scaling card. Once online, every turn you get stronger.
- Inflame — gain 2/3 Strength permanently. Simple, effective, no setup required.
- Spot Weakness — gain 3/4 Strength if enemy intends to attack. Conditional but very efficient.
- Limit Break — double your Strength. Insane with any Strength source. Upgraded, it doesn't exhaust.
- Heavy Blade — deals 14 damage, affected by Strength 3x/5x. The payoff card for Strength builds.

#### Support Cards

- Pummel — multi-hit attack, each hit benefits from Strength
- Sword Boomerang — hits 3/4 random enemies, each hit gets Strength bonus
- Twin Strike — hits twice, double Strength benefit
- Headbutt — damage + puts card on top of draw pile (get Limit Break back quickly)

#### Strengths

- Damage scales infinitely — each turn your attacks hit harder
- Multi-hit attacks amplify Strength enormously
- Simple to pilot — play Strength cards, then play attacks
- Works with almost any attack card in your deck

#### Weaknesses

- Slow to start — Demon Form costs 3 energy and takes turns to build up
- Needs block cards to survive while Strength ramps up
- Vulnerable to Artifact enemies who can prevent debuffs that support Strength strategies

#### Key Relic Synergies

- Vajra — +1 Strength at combat start. Free scaling on every fight.
- Girya — Lift at campfires for +1 Strength permanently. Long-term investment.
- Red Skull — +3 Strength when below 50% HP. Risky but powerful.

### Exhaust Engine

Build a deck around exhausting cards to trigger powerful synergies. Dark Embrace draws cards, Feel No Pain generates block, Dead Branch creates free cards. The exhaust engine can thin your deck to just your best cards while generating massive value.

#### Core Cards

- Corruption — ALL Skills cost 0 but exhaust after play. The centerpiece of exhaust strategies. With Feel No Pain, every skill you play generates block AND draws cards.
- Dark Embrace — whenever a card is exhausted, draw 1 card. Turns exhaust into card advantage.
- Feel No Pain — whenever a card is exhausted, gain 3/4 block. Turns exhaust into defense.
- Sentinel — gain 5/8 block. When exhausted, gain 2/3 energy. Extra energy fuels big turns.
- Second Wind — exhaust ALL non-attack cards in hand, gain 5/7 block per card exhausted. Massive block burst.

#### Support Cards

- Fiend Fire — exhaust your entire hand, deal 7 damage per card exhausted. Finisher card.
- Burning Pact — exhaust 1 card, draw 2/3 cards. Fuel for the engine.
- True Grit — gain 7/9 block, exhaust a card. Block + exhaust trigger.
- Offering — lose 6 HP, gain 2 energy, draw 3/5 cards. Powerful cycle card.
- Havoc — play the top card of draw pile for free, exhaust it. Free value.

#### Strengths

- Self-thinning deck — as you exhaust cards, remaining draws become more consistent
- Massive card advantage with Dark Embrace
- Enormous block generation with Feel No Pain + Corruption
- Can generate more value per turn than almost any other strategy
- Dead Branch makes the engine self-sustaining by replacing exhausted cards

#### Weaknesses

- Requires specific pieces to function — Corruption without Feel No Pain can leave you defenseless
- Can exhaust too many cards and run out of options if engine isn't fully assembled
- Expensive to set up — Corruption costs 3, Dark Embrace costs 2
- Fights that are too short don't give the engine time to start

#### Key Relic Synergies

- Dead Branch — create a random card whenever you exhaust a card. The dream relic for exhaust builds.
- Charon's Ashes — deal 3 damage to ALL enemies whenever you exhaust a card. Free AOE.
- Strange Spoon — 50% chance exhausted cards go to discard instead. Reusable engine pieces.

### Block Engine

A defensive Ironclad build centered around Barricade (block doesn't expire between turns) and Body Slam (deal damage equal to your block). Build up massive block over multiple turns, then one-shot enemies with Body Slam.

#### Core Cards

- Barricade — your block persists between turns. The key enabler — without Barricade, block resets each turn.
- Body Slam — deal damage equal to your current block. 0 cost. The payoff for accumulating block.
- Shrug It Off — gain 8/11 block, draw 1 card. The best Ironclad block card — block + draw.
- Metallicize — gain 3/4 block at end of every turn permanently. Free block that stacks with Barricade.
- Entrench — double your current block. With Barricade, this gets insane quickly.

#### Support Cards

- Impervious — gain 30/40 block. Huge single-turn block gain.
- Flame Barrier — gain 12/16 block, deal 4 damage when attacked. Block + damage.
- Iron Wave — gain 5/7 block and deal 5/7 damage. Versatile but unexciting.
- Power Through — gain 15/20 block but add Wounds to hand. Big block but clutters hand.

#### Strengths

- Nearly invincible once Barricade is online — block accumulates faster than enemies can damage you
- Body Slam provides scaling damage without any attack cards — your block IS your damage
- Very safe and consistent once set up
- Entrench doubles block exponentially — goes from 30 to 60 to 120 to 240...

#### Weaknesses

- Barricade costs 3 energy — slow to get online
- Without Barricade, the entire strategy falls apart
- Vulnerable to enemies that remove block or bypass it
- Slow to kill — Block/Body Slam builds take many turns to win

## Act By Act Plan

### Act1

#### Priorities

- Get frontloaded damage to kill hallway enemies in 2-3 turns (Carnage, Pommel Strike, Headbutt)
- Find at least one scaling source (Inflame, Demon Form, or Spot Weakness)
- Pick up 1-2 block cards beyond starting Defends (Shrug It Off is premium)
- Upgrade Bash to Bash+ (3 Vulnerable is a massive damage increase)
- Remove 1-2 Strikes at shops

**Card Priorities:** Attacks > Scaling > Block. You need to kill things before you need to block.

**Elite Readiness:** Fight your first elite after picking up 2-3 good cards. Bash+ plus a strong attack is usually enough.

**Boss Preparation:** Ensure you have some scaling (even just Inflame) and enough block to survive 5-6 turns.

### Act2

#### Priorities

- Solidify your deck's identity — Strength scaling, Exhaust engine, or Block/Body Slam
- Add key Power cards (Demon Form, Corruption, Barricade) if offered
- Improve block density to handle Act 2's harder enemies
- Remove remaining Strikes and Defends
- Upgrade key cards aggressively

**Card Priorities:** Scaling > Block > Draw. Your deck should have its core strategy by end of Act 2.

**Elite Readiness:** Your deck should handle elites comfortably if your strategy is coming together.

**Boss Preparation:** Ensure your scaling is online and reliable. Act 2 bosses are significantly harder than Act 1.

### Act3

#### Priorities

- Skip most card rewards — your deck is built
- Upgrade remaining key cards at campfires
- Remove any remaining filler cards at shops
- Ensure your deck can handle the Act 3 boss specifically
- Conserve HP for the final boss fight

**Card Priorities:** Only take cards that directly address a weakness against the final boss.

**Focus:** Optimization, not addition. Make your existing cards better, don't add new ones.

## Common Pitfalls

**Too Many Powers:** Don't take every Power card. Powers cost energy to play and don't help you survive the turn you play them. 3-4 Powers is usually enough.

**No Frontload:** Demon Form is amazing but does nothing on the turn you play it. Make sure you have attacks that deal immediate damage.

**Ignoring Block:** Ironclad has the best attacks but mediocre block. Don't neglect defense — Shrug It Off, Impervious, and True Grit are important.

**Exhaust Without Payoff:** Taking Corruption without Feel No Pain or Dark Embrace leaves you without skills to play. Don't start exhausting until you have the payoff pieces.

**Overreliance On Burning Blood:** 6 HP per fight is nice but won't save you from 30+ damage elite fights. Don't take extra damage just because you have healing.

**Heavy Blade Without Strength:** Heavy Blade is mediocre without Strength. It only becomes powerful with 5+ Strength stacks.
